headline: Why do a postdoc? Pay, freedom and public health
description: Three postdocs discuss pay, insecure contracts and academic freedom, including SARS-CoV-2 sequencing in Pakistan and careers in bioinformatics.
summary: Andrew Page asks Dr Emma Waters, Dr Heather Felgate and Dr Muhammad Yasir why they chose postdoctoral research despite lower pay and insecure contracts. Recorded before first-year PhD students on the Microbes, Microbiomes and Bioinformatics doctoral training programme at the Quadram Institute in Norwich, the discussion explores scientific discovery, flexible working and public benefit. The panellists describe what keeps them in research, while Andrew encourages students to keep their career options open.

people.name: Lee Katz
people.affiliation: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention; University of Georgia (adjunct member)

sections.heading: Why stay in postdoctoral research?
sections.body:
Andrew opens with a deliberately blunt question: why accept an underpaid postdoc with long hours when industry might offer two or three times the salary? Emma’s answer is that she loves research: finding a problem, choosing from wet-lab and computational approaches, and solving something nobody has solved before. Discovery and the freedom to explore matter to her.

Emma also explains that pay looks different depending on your starting point. Coming from a disadvantaged background, with nobody else in her family having attended university, she earns more than her parents did. Nevertheless, she recognises that four undergraduate years and five PhD years represent substantial expertise that should be reflected in pay.

sections.heading: Flexibility comes with insecure contracts
sections.body:
Heather values enjoying her work, using her brain and having some control over her hours. She describes being able to work around family responsibilities, including staying home with a sick child and making up time later. She would like better pay and a permanent position, but those wishes sit alongside genuine satisfaction with her current work.

Her grant-funded contract has an end date, however, and the prospect of needing another job in six months is stressful. She also describes a less linear career than moving straight into a permanent post: six months teaching chemistry and biology at a girls’ school in Uganda, and a year in Melbourne running a Mexican restaurant. She sees these experiences as valuable and encourages students to explore life beyond their immediate research path.

sections.heading: Comparing salaries and deciding what matters
sections.body:
An audience member asks whether seeing school friends earn more ever makes the panellists regret staying in research. Emma acknowledges noticing peers reaching managing-director positions and hearing about their salaries. But she also sees stress in their lives, and weighs that against being happy in her own workplace and having flexibility over her day.

Heather frames the decision around what someone wants from life rather than a single correct career choice. If money is what makes a person happy, pursuing it is a valid option. The discussion also touches on being able to express yourself at work and finding satisfaction through public outreach, including encouraging children to consider science.

sections.heading: From difficult experiments to pandemic evidence
sections.body:
Yasir describes the satisfaction of solving an experimental puzzle, but also the misery when a method does not work. One project required six months of difficult optimisation. He credits teamwork, resilience and encouragement with getting through that period; the eventual success changed how the work felt.

During the pandemic, Yasir was given freedom to collaborate independently with his former university in Pakistan. That collaboration sequenced about 600 SARS-CoV-2 samples—almost half of the country’s sequenced samples at that point, according to his account.

Andrew places the work in the context of Pakistan being on the UK’s travel red list. He says there was concern about the Delta variant, whereas their sequencing showed Alpha, which had been imported from the UK. The panel discusses the evidence’s relevance to travel policy and families meeting again. Yasir presents this as an example of academic freedom supporting an international public-health contribution.

sections.heading: Keep collaboration and career options open
sections.body:
Heather values being able to contact unfamiliar researchers, discuss projects and propose collaborations or papers. She contrasts that openness with the intellectual-property restrictions she associates with industry. Yasir adds that researchers can seek grants and funding to expand their work or move towards greater responsibility.

Andrew closes with practical advice for students concerned about earnings: keep options open, and consider the bioinformatics and data science route rather than focusing solely on laboratory work. He argues that it generally offers more earning potential and more opportunities in industry. The panel’s broader message is to choose according to personal priorities, not salary alone.

faq.q: Why choose a postdoc over a better-paid industry job?
faq.a: The panellists value discovery, enjoyable work, flexibility and opportunities to help people through research. They acknowledge the pay gap, but emphasise that the right choice depends on personal priorities.

faq.q: What drawbacks of postdoctoral work does the panel discuss?
faq.a: Lower pay and insecure contracts are central concerns. Heather describes the stress of knowing a grant-funded job will end, while Yasir discusses the emotional difficulty of spending months on an experimental method that is not working.

faq.q: What did Yasir’s SARS-CoV-2 collaboration in Pakistan contribute?
faq.a: The collaboration sequenced about 600 samples, which Yasir says represented almost half of Pakistan’s sequenced samples at that time. Andrew explains that the findings provided evidence relevant to UK travel restrictions, showing Alpha rather than the feared Delta variant in their sequencing.

faq.q: What career advice does Andrew give bioinformatics PhD students?
faq.a: Andrew recommends keeping career options open. For students prioritising earnings, he suggests bioinformatics and data science rather than a solely laboratory-focused route, arguing that these offer greater earning potential and more opportunities in industry.
